name: Operation Ivy
label: Lookout!
lede: Two years, about 185 shows, one album cut in a day, and a Gilman Street sound that fed Rancid and half of third-wave ska.

eras.title: A garage, a gym and four Berkeley kids
eras.text: Tim Armstrong and Matt Freeman had already played together in Basic Radio. With singer Jesse Michaels and drummer Dave Mello they became Operation Ivy in May 1987, and 924 Gilman Street was the room that made them.

years.h: Operation Ivy starts in Dave Mello's garage
years.p: Wikipedia dates the first show to May 27, 1987, in Mello's garage, with a first Gilman Street set the next day. Members: Michaels, Armstrong, Freeman, Mello.
years.xp:
Armstrong and Freeman had played together in the Berkeley ska-punk band Basic Radio. Larry Livermore's account says the two first shared a stage at an Albany High talent show in 1983.

Livermore also says Mello started out on a double-bass-drum kit until Freeman made him drop one and learn a plain four-on-the-floor beat.

years.h: Two songs on the Maximumrocknroll comp Turn It Around!
years.p: "I Got No" and "Officer" are Operation Ivy's first appearance on vinyl, on a Gilman Street compilation from Maximumrocknroll.

eras.title: Hectic
eras.text: Lookout Records put out a six-song 7-inch, and the band became the first Gilman act to tour the country. By mid-1988 Gilman was too small for them.

years.h: Hectic EP: six songs, one day, Lookout Records
years.p: Larry Livermore's label issued the EP with about 1,000 copies in the first pressing. It became one of Lookout's best-sellers.
years.xp: Livermore says the pressing sold out within a month. Wikipedia calls Hectic one of Lookout's best-selling records.

years.h: Operation Ivy is the first Gilman band to tour the country
years.p: Livermore booked a six-week trip across the US in a 1969 Chrysler Newport.
years.xp: According to Livermore, they played to three people in El Paso and in Lexington, Kentucky. Back in May at Gilman, the crowds were huge and some old scenesters began heckling them as ska boys.

years.h: "Hangin' Out" lands on The Thing That Ate Floyd
years.p: Lookout's compilation carries the band's only other 1988 release, next to Bay Area label mates.

eras.title: Energy, and the end
eras.text: They cut one album in days, then chose to stop before a major label could turn them into something else. The last show was in May 1989 at Gilman.

years.h: Energy: 19 songs recorded live at Sound and Vision, San Francisco
years.p: Producer Kevin Army got the basic tracks down in a single eight-hour session, one or two takes per song.
years.xp:
Army put the band in a semicircle in the tiny room, left the drum room door open for reverb and overdubbed Mello's snares in his bathroom. Paul Bany added saxophone to "Bad Town". Army says he talked the band out of gang shouts on every song by comparing it to the Village People.

Rolling Stone also reports that Moon Records had passed on the demos because they did not fit its 2 Tone ska brand.

q: It sort of wasn't that fun anymore.
years.h: The band decides to quit while it is still a Gilman band
years.p: Wikipedia reports an EMI offer; the band split rather than take the deal.
years.xp:
Freeman told Livermore the band had stopped being fun and felt too serious. Armstrong says he and Michaels talked it over at a Telegraph Avenue volleyball court as a mutual decision.

Wikipedia says the band had played about 185 shows and recorded 32 songs.

years.h: Last show at Gilman: over 1,000 in a room for 300
years.p: Livermore puts the crowd past 1,000, in a room with a legal capacity of 300. Green Day played their first show under that name the same night.
years.xp: Wikipedia says an unofficial encore followed the next day in a friend's Pinole backyard.

years.p: Lookout issued the album as the band was breaking up; sources differ on March versus later in 1989.

eras.title: The band that grew after it ended
eras.text: Armstrong and Freeman formed Rancid; Michaels started Big Rig and later Common Rider. Meanwhile the records kept selling and a wave of ska bands cited them.

years.h: Lookout collects everything on one 27-song CD
years.p: The compilation gathers Energy, Hectic and the Turn It Around! tracks, and becomes how most fans hear the band.

years.h: Take Warning tribute: Reel Big Fish, Aquabats and more
years.p: Bands including Reel Big Fish ("Unity") and Cherry Poppin' Daddies ("Sound System") covered the songs.

eras.title: Gold, a lost label, a stage reunion
eras.text: Energy passed a gold certification, left Lookout under a royalty dispute, and the members shared a stage once more.

years.h: Energy is certified gold by the RIAA
years.p: Wikipedia lists the certification more than fourteen years after the band split.
Wikipedia says the label removed it from its catalog, as other Lookout bands had also left over money.

q: To go back 20 years wouldn't feel right.
years.h: Jesse Michaels joins Rancid to play two Op Ivy songs
years.p: At the Warfield Theatre in San Francisco he sang "Unity" and "Sound System", his first stage appearance with them in over 15 years.
years.xp: Michaels has said reunion prospects were poor and that the band never belonged in a big rock club. Armstrong said going back twenty years would not feel right.

years.p: Armstrong's Hellcat imprint at Epitaph issued it remastered, and put out red and clear vinyl of both Energy and Hectic in April 2012.

years.h: Michaels and Armstrong record together for the first time in 24 years
years.p: They cut "Living in a Dangerous Land" for Armstrong's Tim Timebomb and Friends series.

years.h: Documentary Turn It Around tells the East Bay story
years.p: The film about the East Bay punk scene features Operation Ivy and Gilman Street.

years.h: Armstrong and Michaels form DOOM Regulator
years.p: With Circle Jerks drummer Joey Castillo the pair started a new band, briefly announced as Bad Optix.

years.h: Laura Jane Grace and Catbite release a live Op Ivy set
years.p: Operation Ivy: Live at the Empty Bottle has 27 songs recorded at a Chicago Riot Fest afterparty in September 2024.
